title: WSET Level 2 mock exam: 50 free practice questions
summary: An unofficial 50-question mock exam in the style of the WSET Level 2 Award in Wines: grapes, regions, winemaking, sparkling, fortified, labels and service.

questions.q: Which part of the grape gives the winemaker most of the sugar, acid and water that end up in a wine?
questions.why: The pulp, or flesh, is mostly water and holds the grape's sugars and acids, plus some flavour. That sugar is what the yeast later turns into alcohol.
questions.deeper: The skin supplies colour, tannin and many aroma compounds, which is why red wines ferment with their skins. Seeds and stems add tannin, often of a harsher kind.

questions.q: What happens to black grapes at véraison?
opts: The vine flowers and the tiny berries set
The berries change colour and start to ripen
The ripe grapes are picked for the harvest
The leaves drop and the vine goes dormant
questions.why: Véraison is the moment the berries stop simply growing and start ripening. Black grapes turn from green to red and purple, soften, and begin to build up sugar.
questions.deeper: Flowering and fruit set come earlier in the season. White grapes go through véraison too; they just turn from hard green to a softer, more translucent yellow-green.

questions.q: As grapes ripen on the vine, how do their sugar and acid levels usually change?
questions.why: During ripening the grape fills with sugar while its acidity drops. That is why very ripe grapes make wines with more alcohol and less acidity.
questions.deeper: The tannins in the skins ripen too, becoming less green and bitter. Picking early keeps more acidity, at the cost of some ripeness and potential alcohol.

questions.q: A French wine is labelled 'IGP Pays d'Oc'. Which EU category does IGP correspond to?
opts: A classified growth, such as Grand Cru
questions.why: IGP (Indication Géographique Protégée) is the French term for the EU's PGI category. It sits below PDO, which in France is labelled AOC or AOP.
questions.deeper: Pays d'Oc, covering Languedoc-Roussillon, is a large IGP where producers are allowed to put the grape variety and vintage on the label, so you will often see 'Pays d'Oc Merlot' or 'Pays d'Oc Chardonnay'.

questions.q: What makes the grapes used for Sauternes so sweet and concentrated?
opts: They are frozen on the vine before picking
They are dried on mats after the harvest
They are affected by noble rot (botrytis)
They have grape spirit added to the juice
questions.why: Sauternes relies on Botrytis cinerea, or noble rot. Autumn mists from the Ciron and Garonne rivers let the fungus develop, then the afternoon sun dries the grapes, so they shrivel and their sugar and flavour concentrate.
questions.deeper: The main grape is Semillon, usually with some Sauvignon Blanc. Freezing on the vine is how Icewine (Eiswein) is made, and drying grapes after picking is the method behind Recioto della Valpolicella.

questions.q: What does malolactic conversion do to a wine?
opts: It turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid
It turns the grape sugar into alcohol and gas
It draws extra tannin out of the grape seeds
It removes the dead yeast cells left after fermentation
questions.why: Bacteria convert tart, green-apple-like malic acid into milder lactic acid, so the wine tastes softer and rounder. It can also add buttery flavours.
questions.deeper: Almost all red wines go through it. For whites it is a style choice: many Chardonnays do, while Riesling producers usually block it to keep the wine crisp.

questions.q: When making a red wine, when are the grapes normally pressed?
opts: After fermentation, once colour and tannin are extracted
Before fermentation, so only the clear juice is fermented
Only after the wine has spent a year in oak
Never: red grapes are not pressed at all
questions.why: Red wine gets its colour and tannin from the skins, so the juice ferments in contact with them. Pressing comes after, or near the end of, fermentation to separate the new wine from the skins.
questions.deeper: White wine is the opposite: the grapes are pressed first and only the juice is fermented. That is how a white wine can be made from black grapes, as happens in Champagne.

questions.q: How do most still rosé wines get their pink colour?
opts: From ageing a white wine in toasted oak barrels
From a short period of skin contact with black grapes
From fermenting white grape juice at a much warmer temperature
From adding red grape juice just before bottling
questions.why: Black grapes are crushed and left with their skins for a short time, typically hours rather than days, before the juice is drawn off and fermented. The longer the contact, the deeper the pink.
questions.deeper: Blending a little red wine into white is the other method. It is rarely used for still rosé, and EU rules forbid it for wines without a PDO or PGI, but it is common for rosé Champagne.

questions.q: A red wine is aged for many years in bottle. How does its colour usually change?
opts: It grows darker and more intensely purple with time
It takes on a pale lemon-green colour
It loses depth and turns towards orange and brown
It stays exactly as it was when bottled
questions.why: Over time the colour pigments drop out, so an aged red becomes paler and develops orange, then brown, tones, most visibly at the rim. The tannins soften at the same time.
questions.deeper: White wines change too, but the other way round: they darken with age, moving towards gold and eventually brown.

questions.q: A wine labelled Chablis Premier Cru is made from which grape?
questions.why: All Chablis is 100% Chardonnay. The cool climate of this northern corner of Burgundy gives a dry wine with high acidity, green apple and citrus fruit, and a steely, often flinty feel.
questions.deeper: Chablis has four levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru. Most Chablis shows little oak influence, which is why it tastes so different from a rich, oaky Chardonnay from a warm region.

questions.q: A Chardonnay smells of vanilla, toast and smoke as well as fruit. Which winemaking choice most likely caused this?
opts: Maturing it in new, small oak barrels
Fermenting it in stainless steel tanks
Ageing it in old, large oak casks
Fermenting it at a very cool temperature
questions.why: New oak gives the most flavour, and small barrels have more wood surface per litre of wine, so new small barrels add the strongest vanilla, toast and smoky notes. How heavily the inside of the barrel is toasted shapes these flavours too.
questions.deeper: Old or large oak vessels add little flavour, and stainless steel adds none, keeping the pure fruit. A cool fermentation tends to give fresh, fruity aromas rather than toasty ones.

questions.q: Which flavours are most typical of Chardonnay from a hot climate?
opts: Green apple, pear and sharp lemon
Tropical fruit like banana and mango
questions.why: Chardonnay is a fairly neutral grape that mirrors its climate. Cool regions give green apple, pear and citrus; moderate ones bring stone fruit and melon; very warm regions push it towards tropical fruit like banana, mango and fig.
questions.deeper: Black pepper and red berries belong to black grapes. Many people mistake the vanilla of oak, or the buttery notes of malolactic conversion, for the taste of the grape itself.

questions.q: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé face each other across the Loire. Which grape makes their white wines?
questions.why: Both are classic Loire Sauvignon Blanc: dry and high in acidity, with green fruit such as gooseberry and green apple, often with a smoky or flinty edge.
questions.deeper: Don't mix up Pouilly-Fumé with Pouilly-Fuissé. Pouilly-Fuissé is in Burgundy's Mâconnais and is made from Chardonnay.

questions.q: Dry white wines from Graves and Pessac-Léognan in Bordeaux are usually Sauvignon Blanc blended with which grape?
questions.why: White Bordeaux is usually a blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon. Sauvignon brings fresh acidity and aroma, while Semillon adds body and texture.
questions.deeper: The same two grapes, shrivelled by noble rot, make the sweet wines of Sauternes, which lies within the Graves area.

questions.q: Which of these German Prädikat levels is made from the ripest grapes at harvest?
questions.why: In order of the grape ripeness they require, the levels run Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, then Beerenauslese (BA), with Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) at the very top. BA is made from selected overripe berries, often touched by noble rot, and is a lusciously sweet wine.
questions.deeper: The Prädikat measures the sugar in the grapes, not in the finished wine, so a Kabinett, Spätlese or Auslese can be dry or sweet. Eiswein needs at least BA-level ripeness, from grapes frozen on the vine.

questions.q: What does 'trocken' tell you on a German wine label?
opts: The grapes froze on the vine
questions.why: Trocken means dry, and halbtrocken ('half-dry') means off-dry. These words describe the sugar left in the finished wine.
questions.deeper: Because the Prädikat level describes the grapes, a 'Spätlese trocken' is a dry wine made from riper-than-usual grapes.

questions.q: Clare Valley and Eden Valley in South Australia are best known for which style of wine?
opts: Rich, buttery Chardonnay aged in new oak
Dry Riesling with lime and high acidity
questions.why: These relatively cool areas are Australia's classic homes of dry Riesling: lean and high in acidity, with a typical lime note when young. With bottle age they develop toast and honey.
questions.deeper: Older Australian Rieslings can also show a petrol or kerosene note, which many tasters see as a sign of quality rather than a fault.

questions.q: Compared with a typical Pinot Grigio from north-east Italy, a Pinot Gris from Alsace is usually...
opts: Lighter in body and more neutral
Grassier and greener, like Sauvignon Blanc
Aged for years in new oak barrels
questions.why: Italian Pinot Grigio is often picked early to keep fresh acidity, giving light, crisp wines with a fairly neutral flavour. In Alsace the grape ripens further and makes medium- to full-bodied wines with richer fruit and a spicy note.
questions.deeper: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape. Key Italian sources include the Delle Venezie DOC and Friuli-Venezia Giulia.

questions.q: In Pauillac and Margaux, on Bordeaux's Left Bank, which grape usually leads the red blend?
questions.why: The Haut-Médoc villages such as Pauillac and Margaux are Cabernet Sauvignon country. It is the main grape, almost always blended with others such as Merlot and Cabernet Franc.
questions.deeper: On the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, the roles swap and Merlot usually takes the lead.

questions.q: Which Australian region is especially famous for Cabernet Sauvignon grown on red 'terra rossa' soil?
questions.why: Coonawarra's narrow strip of bright red terra rossa soil over limestone is famous for Cabernet Sauvignon with intense blackcurrant fruit, sometimes with a mint or eucalyptus note.
questions.deeper: Margaret River in Western Australia is the other big Australian name for Cabernet. Barossa Valley is best known for Shiraz, and Yarra Valley for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

questions.q: Which description best fits a classic Cabernet Sauvignon?
opts: Deep colour, high tannin and acidity, blackcurrant
Pale colour, low tannin, red cherry and strawberry
Deep colour, soft tannin, low acidity, ripe plum
Pale colour, high acidity, citrus and blossom
questions.why: Cabernet Sauvignon has small, thick-skinned berries, which give deep colour and high tannin, along with noticeable acidity. Blackcurrant is its signature fruit, often with mint or green pepper notes in cooler sites.
questions.deeper: It ripens late, so it needs a moderate or warm climate. Its firm structure is one reason it is so often blended with softer Merlot.

questions.q: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol lie on Bordeaux's Right Bank. Which grape usually makes up most of their red blends?
questions.why: Merlot usually makes up the majority of the blend on the Right Bank: roughly 60% in Saint-Émilion and around 80% in Pomerol, often partnered by Cabernet Franc.
questions.deeper: Merlot ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, which makes it a safer bet in a cool year. Malbec is a minor Bordeaux grape that found fame in Argentina.

questions.q: Why is Merlot so often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon?
opts: It adds extra tannin and acidity to a soft Cabernet
It makes the blend lighter in colour and more floral
It ripens later, so it can be picked after Cabernet
Its softer tannin and fleshy fruit round out Cabernet
questions.why: Merlot typically has medium tannin and juicy plum and black cherry fruit, so it softens and fills out Cabernet Sauvignon, which is firmer and higher in tannin. It also ripens earlier, which spreads the grower's risk.
questions.deeper: In cooler sites Merlot leans towards red fruit and plum; in moderate ones, towards blackberry, black plum and black cherry.

questions.q: Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie and Crozes-Hermitage in the Northern Rhône make their red wines mainly from which grape?
questions.why: The Northern Rhône is Syrah's home. Its reds are deep in colour, with blackberry fruit and a typical black pepper note; Hermitage is the most famous of them.
questions.deeper: Grenache rules further south, in the Southern Rhône, where Côtes du Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape are mostly Grenache-led blends.

questions.q: Compared with a Northern Rhône Syrah, a typical Barossa Valley Shiraz is usually...
opts: Riper and fuller, with more alcohol
Paler, lighter and higher in acidity
Leaner, with more black pepper and herbs
Sweet, because fermentation is stopped early
questions.why: The Barossa is hot, so its Shiraz gets very ripe: full-bodied and high in alcohol, with ripe tannins, jammy black fruit and notes like liquorice and dark chocolate. Northern Rhône Syrah, from a more moderate climate, tends to be more restrained and peppery.
questions.deeper: Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape. Producers outside Australia sometimes pick the name to signal style: 'Shiraz' suggests riper and bolder, 'Syrah' more restrained.

questions.q: Red wines from Gevrey-Chambertin, Nuits-Saint-Georges and Pommard are made from which grape?
questions.why: These are village appellations in Burgundy's Côte d'Or, and red Burgundy is Pinot Noir. Expect a paler red with red cherry and raspberry fruit that turns earthy and mushroomy with age.
questions.deeper: Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges are in the Côte de Nuits, Pommard in the Côte de Beaune. Gamay belongs to Beaujolais, just to the south.

questions.q: In Burgundy's classification, which label term marks the very best vineyard sites?
questions.why: From the top down, Burgundy runs Grand Cru, Premier Cru, village wines (such as Pommard) and regional wines (Bourgogne). Grand Crus are a tiny slice, only about 1–2% of production.
questions.deeper: Cru Bourgeois is a Bordeaux term, used in the Médoc. In Chablis, too, the top vineyards are Grand Cru.

questions.q: Which of these New World regions is best known for Pinot Noir?
questions.why: Pinot Noir is the leading grape of Central Otago, on New Zealand's South Island. Pinot needs a cool to moderate climate; in hot places it loses its delicate red-fruit character.
questions.deeper: Barossa is about Shiraz, Coonawarra about Cabernet Sauvignon and Mendoza about Malbec. Other New World Pinot regions to know include Martinborough, Oregon, Yarra Valley and Casablanca Valley.

questions.q: Fleurie is one of the ten Beaujolais crus. Which grape is it made from?
questions.why: Red Beaujolais is made from Gamay, a thin-skinned grape that gives low-tannin wines with bright red fruit such as raspberry and cherry. The crus, including Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent, are the top tier, above Beaujolais-Villages and basic Beaujolais.
questions.deeper: Light, fruity reds like simple Beaujolais are among the few red wines that are happily served lightly chilled.

questions.q: Red Châteauneuf-du-Pape, in the Southern Rhône, is usually a blend led by which grape?
questions.why: Grenache is the backbone of most Châteauneuf-du-Pape, usually with Syrah for colour and spice and Mourvèdre for structure. Grenache thrives in the warm south, giving ripe red fruit, spice and high alcohol.
questions.deeper: In Spain the same grape is called Garnacha and is important in Rioja, Navarra and Priorat.

questions.q: Which of these Rioja label terms promises the longest minimum ageing before release?
questions.why: The ladder runs Joven (little or no ageing), Crianza, Reserva and then Gran Reserva. A red Gran Reserva needs at least five years of ageing in total, including at least two in oak barrels.
questions.deeper: For red Rioja, Crianza needs at least two years in total and Reserva at least three, each with a minimum of one year in oak. The main grape is Tempranillo, often blended with Garnacha.

questions.q: Barolo is made from Nebbiolo. Which description fits it best?
opts: Deep purple, with soft tannin and low acid
Fairly pale, but high in tannin and acidity
Light and low in tannin, best drunk young
Inky black, with low acidity and jammy fruit
questions.why: Nebbiolo is a paradox: its wines look fairly pale and soon turn brick-orange at the rim, yet they are very high in tannin and acidity. Red cherry, rose and tar are its classic aromas, and the best Barolos need years to soften.
questions.deeper: Barbaresco, also in Piedmont, is 100% Nebbiolo too. Here a pale colour is no sign of a light wine.

questions.q: Brunello di Montalcino is made from which grape?
questions.why: Brunello di Montalcino, from Tuscany, must be 100% Sangiovese. The grape gives high acidity, medium to high tannin and red cherry fruit, often with savoury, herbal notes.
questions.deeper: Sangiovese is also the main grape of Chianti and Chianti Classico. The grape called Montepulciano is a different variety, best known in Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.

questions.q: What makes Amarone della Valpolicella so different from a basic Valpolicella?
opts: Grape spirit is added during fermentation
The grapes are frozen on the vine
Its grapes are dried before fermenting
It is aged under a layer of flor yeast
questions.why: For Amarone, Corvina-based grapes are dried for a period after harvest, which concentrates their sugar and flavour. Fermented to dryness, they make a full-bodied red with high alcohol, often over 15%, and raisined, dried-fruit flavours.
questions.deeper: If the fermentation stops early, the same dried grapes give sweet Recioto della Valpolicella. Basic Valpolicella is light, fresh and fruity.

questions.q: What does 'Classico' mean on an Italian label such as Chianti Classico or Soave Classico?
opts: The wine was aged for at least five years
The wine is made only from old vines
The wine is a blend of several grape varieties
The wine comes from the historic heart of the region
questions.why: Classico marks the original, historic zone of a wine region, its traditional heartland, from before the area was enlarged. Chianti Classico, for example, sits on the hills between Florence and Siena.
questions.deeper: It is about place, not ageing. For extra ageing on an Italian label, look for 'Riserva'.

questions.q: Mendoza, where many vineyards sit high in the foothills of the Andes, is best known for which grape?
questions.why: Malbec is Mendoza's most important grape. The high-altitude vineyards get intense sunshine, giving deep-coloured, full-bodied reds with ripe black fruit.
questions.deeper: Carmenère is Chile's signature grape, Pinotage South Africa's, and Zinfandel is a big name in California.

questions.q: On a South African wine label, what does 'Cape Blend' usually tell you?
opts: It is a sweet wine from Constantia
It is a sparkling wine made like Champagne
It is a blend of wines from several vintages
It is a red blend that includes Pinotage
questions.why: A Cape Blend is a South African red blend that includes Pinotage. There is no strict legal rule for how much, but Pinotage is expected to be a good share of the mix, often quoted as 30–70%. Pinotage is South Africa's own grape, a cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.
questions.deeper: South Africa's traditional-method sparkling wine has its own term: Cap Classique.

questions.q: Condrieu, in the Northern Rhône, makes white wine from which grape?
questions.why: Condrieu is made only from Viognier and is the grape's most famous home. Viognier gives full-bodied whites with intense peach, apricot and blossom aromas.
questions.deeper: Condrieu is a white-only island in a region best known for red Syrah.

questions.q: Vouvray, in the Loire Valley, is made from which grape?
questions.why: Vouvray is Chenin Blanc country. Chenin's high acidity lets it make every style, from dry through off-dry and sweet to sparkling, so check the label for words like sec or demi-sec.
questions.deeper: In warm years noble rot can give lusciously sweet Vouvray. South Africa's Western Cape is the other big name for Chenin Blanc.

questions.q: Tokaji Aszú is a famous sweet wine from Hungary. Which grape is it mainly made from?
questions.why: Furmint is the key grape of Tokaj. For Aszú, berries shrivelled by noble rot are picked one by one, crushed to a paste and soaked in must or wine, giving a sweet wine kept fresh by high acidity.
questions.deeper: Semillon is the noble-rot grape of Sauternes, not Tokaji. The word Aszú on the label is your clue to the botrytised sweet style.

questions.q: Which three grapes are the most widely planted in Champagne?
opts: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris
questions.why: Pinot Noir covers about 38% of Champagne's vineyards, and Chardonnay and Meunier about 31% each. Most Champagnes are blends of these three.
questions.deeper: Glera is the grape of Prosecco, which is made by a different method.

questions.q: Cava from Spain gets its bubbles in the same way as Champagne. What does that mean?
opts: The second fermentation happens in a sealed tank
Carbon dioxide is pumped into the finished wine
Sugar is added just before the wine is served
The second fermentation happens in the bottle
questions.why: Only traditional-method wines can be labelled Cava. A second fermentation takes place inside each bottle; the yeast sediment is then gathered in the neck and removed. Time on these lees adds bready, toasty notes.
questions.deeper: The tank method is used for Prosecco and Asti instead. South Africa calls its traditional-method sparkling wine Cap Classique.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly describes Prosecco?
opts: Pinot Noir grapes, aged under flor
questions.why: Prosecco is made mainly from Glera, and its second fermentation takes place in large sealed tanks (the Martinotti or Charmat method). This keeps the fresh, fruity aromas of pear, apple and flowers.
questions.deeper: Small amounts of other grapes are allowed. The tank method is quicker than bottle fermentation and suits wines meant to be drunk young.

questions.q: Which description best fits a classic Asti DOCG?
opts: Dry and crisp, made from Glera grapes
Sweet, low in alcohol, made from Moscato
A still, full-bodied red from Piedmont
questions.why: Classic Asti is made from Moscato (Muscat) in a single fermentation in sealed tanks. The fermentation is stopped early, so the wine stays sweet, low in alcohol (usually about 7–9%) and full of fresh, grapey aromas.
questions.deeper: There is no second fermentation: the carbon dioxide from that one fermentation is trapped in the tank and becomes the bubbles. The rules now also allow drier and traditional-method versions, but the sweet, tank-made style is the one to know. Glera is the grape of Prosecco.

questions.q: What gives Fino Sherry its pale colour and fresh, bready, almond-like character?
opts: Ageing in contact with air for many years
Ageing under a layer of flor yeast
questions.why: Fino is fortified to about 15% after fermentation, a strength at which a layer of flor yeast can grow on the wine in the cask. The flor shields the wine from oxygen and adds bready, almond notes, so it stays pale and dry.
questions.deeper: Oloroso is fortified higher, so flor cannot survive, and it ages in contact with oxygen, turning brown and nutty. Sweet styles such as Cream are sweetened after fermentation.

questions.q: When is grape spirit added in Port production?
opts: Partway through fermentation, to stop it
After fermentation, once the wine is dry
Only when the Port is bottled
questions.why: The spirit is added while the must is still fermenting. This stops the fermentation, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine, which ends up sweet and around 19–22% alcohol.
questions.deeper: Sherry is the opposite: spirit goes in after fermentation, so most Sherries start out dry. For Port the usual ratio is about one part spirit to four parts wine.

questions.q: Why should bottles closed with a cork be stored lying on their side?
opts: To let the sediment settle on the cork
To keep the cork moist so it stays airtight
So the wine can breathe slowly through the cork
To speed up the ageing of the wine
questions.why: Lying the bottle down keeps the wine in contact with the cork, so the cork stays moist and seals well. A dried-out cork can shrink and let in oxygen, which spoils the wine.
questions.deeper: Good storage is also cool and steady in temperature (roughly 10–15 °C) and dark, because light can damage wine, especially delicate whites in clear glass.

questions.q: WSET recommends serving which of these wines lightly chilled?
opts: A sweet, botrytised wine such as Sauternes
A sparkling wine such as Prosecco
A full-bodied red wine such as Barolo
A full-bodied white such as Meursault
questions.why: WSET's guidance is to serve full-bodied whites, often oaked ones like Meursault, lightly chilled (around 10–13 °C). Served too cold, their rich aromas and flavours are muted.
questions.deeper: Sweet and sparkling wines are served well chilled, light- and medium-bodied whites and rosés chilled, and medium- and full-bodied reds at room temperature. Light-bodied reds can be served at room temperature or lightly chilled.

questions.q: A wine smells musty and mouldy, like a damp cellar, and its fruit seems dull. What is the most likely fault?
questions.why: These are the classic signs of cork taint, usually caused by a compound called TCA. A 'corked' wine smells musty or mouldy and its fruit aromas are muted.
questions.deeper: The fault is in that bottle, not the wine itself, so another bottle of the same wine should be fine. Heat damage shows differently, with stewed, cooked-fruit flavours.

questions.q: What effect does chilli heat in a dish have on the wine served with it?
opts: It makes the wine taste sweeter and softer
It increases the burning feel of the alcohol
It makes tannic red wines taste much smoother
It makes the wine taste less acidic
questions.why: Chilli heat and alcohol amplify each other, so a high-alcohol wine with a spicy dish can feel fiery and hot.
questions.deeper: Lower-alcohol wines are a safer choice with spicy food; a touch of sweetness, as in an off-dry Riesling, can help too.
